bmt-2022-geometry-05.title: Back wheels as cone bases
bmt-2022-geometry-05.body:
Each back wheel is the base of a cone whose apex is the common center of the circles traced on the ground; the radius of the traced circle equals the slant height of that cone.

The two back wheels bound a frustum of height $40$ and base radii $10$ and $9$, so its slant height is $\sqrt{(10-9)^2+40^2}=\sqrt{1601}$. The slant heights $L_{10}$ and $L_9$ of the two cones satisfy $L_{10}-L_9=\sqrt{1601}$ and $\frac{L_9}{L_{10}}=\frac9{10}$, so $L_{10}=10\sqrt{1601}$ and $L_9=9\sqrt{1601}$.

The front wheel traces a circle of radius $\frac{19\sqrt{1601}}2$, of length $19\pi\sqrt{1601}$. Its circumference is $60\pi$, so it makes $\frac{19\sqrt{1601}}{60}$ rotations, i.e. $\frac{19\sqrt{1601}}{60}\cdot360=114\sqrt{1601}$ degrees.

**Answer: $114\sqrt{1601}$ degrees**

bmt-2022-geometry-07.title: Express $AH$ with the circumradius
bmt-2022-geometry-07.body:
Let $R$ be the circumradius and $\alpha=\angle BAC$. A standard fact: $AH=2R\cos\alpha$ (derived by dropping the altitude from $B$ to $E$ on $CA$: $AH=\frac{AE}{\sin\angle AHE}=\frac{AB\cos\alpha}{\sin C}=2R\cos\alpha$).

The distance from $Y$ to $AC$ is $AY\sin\frac\alpha2$, so $\sin\frac\alpha2=\frac{\sqrt{15}}6$ and $\cos\alpha=1-2\sin^2\frac\alpha2=1-\frac{30}{36}=\frac16$.

Then $4=2R\cdot\frac16$ gives $R=12$. Also $\sin\alpha=\sqrt{1-\frac1{36}}=\frac{\sqrt{35}}6$, so $BC=2R\sin\alpha=24\cdot\frac{\sqrt{35}}6=4\sqrt{35}$.

**Answer: $4\sqrt{35}$**

bmt-2022-geometry-08.title: An infinite product of secants
bmt-2022-geometry-08.body:
If a regular $m$-gon is circumscribed about a circle of radius $r$, its circumradius is $r\sec\frac\pi m$. So the radius of $\omega_n$ is $\sec\frac\pi4\sec\frac\pi8\cdots\sec\frac\pi{2^n}$.

Using $2\sin x=\sin 2x\sec x$ repeatedly (with $\sin\frac\pi2=1$):
$$\sec\tfrac\pi4\cdots\sec\tfrac\pi{2^n}=2^{n-1}\sin\tfrac\pi{2^n}.$$
As $n\to\infty$, $2^{n-1}\sin\frac\pi{2^n}\to\frac\pi2$ (since $\sin t\sim t$). So the limiting radius is $\frac\pi2$ and $A=\pi\left(\frac\pi2\right)^2=\frac{\pi^3}4$.

**Answer: $\frac{\pi^3}{4}$**

bmt-2022-geometry-09.title: Radical axes and radical centers
bmt-2022-geometry-09.body:
For two spheres the plane of their intersection circle is their radical plane. For three spheres $A,B,C$ the three radical planes share a line (the radical axis), and for four spheres $A,B,C,D$ all six radical planes pass through one point (the radical center).

So a set of four planes surely has a common point in two situations:

1. It contains the three planes of some triple of spheres (they meet in a line) plus any other plane: $\binom73$ triples times the other $\binom72-3=18$ planes: $35\cdot18=630$. (A set cannot contain two different such triples, so there is no double counting.)
2. It consists of four of the six planes from one set of four spheres, with no three of them from the same triple of spheres: choose the four spheres, $\binom74=35$, and then $\binom64-4\cdot3=3$ four-plane subsets (the 4-cycles of $K_4$). That gives $35\cdot3=105$.

The conditions on the centers allow a configuration where no other four planes meet, so the least possible number is $630+105=735$.

**Answer: 735**

bmt-2022-geometry-10.title: Radical axis
bmt-2022-geometry-10.body:
Let $M$ be the midpoint of $BC$; $BFEC$ is cyclic with diameter $BC$ (centre $M$). We claim $XY$ is the radical axis of the point-circle $A$ and circle $(BFEC)$.

$X$: $XA$ is tangent to $(ABC)$, so $XA^2=XB\cdot XC$, the powers of $X$ with respect to $A$ and $(BFEC)$ agree. $Y$: $\angle YAC=\angle ACB=\angle AFE$, so $YA$ is tangent to circle $(AFHE)$ and $YA^2=YE\cdot YF$, again the two powers agree.

Hence $XY\perp AM$; let $T=XY\cap AM$. Compute: $AX^2=XB\cdot XC=4\cdot12=48$, so $AX=4\sqrt3$. Since $\triangle AFE\sim\triangle ACB$ and $\triangle AFEY\sim\triangle ACBX$, $\frac{AY}{AX}=\frac{EF}{BC}=\frac{\sqrt3}2$, so $AY=6$. Also $MX=XB+\frac{BC}2=8$.

From $AY\parallel MX$: $\triangle ATY\sim\triangle MTX$, so $\frac{TX}{TY}=\frac{MX}{AY}=\frac43$. From the right angle at $T$: $AX^2-TX^2=AY^2-TY^2$, i.e. $48-TX^2=36-TY^2$. Solving gives $TX=\frac{8\sqrt{21}}7$ and $TY=\frac{6\sqrt{21}}7$, so $XY=TX+TY=2\sqrt{21}$.

**Answer: $2\sqrt{21}$**
